The final effluent meter only includes the volume of water that is pumped to the distribution system, which does not include the streams that flow to the sanitary sewer from upstream processes.

The WRRF has many uncovered processes with a total surface area over 200,000 square feet. The processes consist of two primary clarifiers (5,654 sq.ft), an EQ Basin (104,544 sq.ft), a biofilter (31,416 sq.ft), a secondary clarifier (15,394 sq.ft), a supernatant holding lagoon (15,000 sq.ft), two aeration basins (7,360 sq.ft), two final clarifiers (10,053 sq.ft), two EQ tanks (8,970 sq.ft), and four filter cells (960 sq.ft) which are all exposed to rainfall intrusion and/or rainwater runoff. The total process square footage does not account for the areas at the WRRF that are within containment. Containment areas gravity flow to multiple sumps throughout the plant which pump back to the beginning of the treatment process after the Parshall flumes where influent is totalized. To add, treated process water (3W) is used for washdowns. 3W makes up a portion of the effluent; however, this water is not metered and cannot be extrapolated from our effluent flow.

The WRRF has many uncovered processes with a total surface area over 200,000 square feet. The processes consist of two primary clarifiers (5,654 sq.ft), an EQ Basin (104,544 sq.ft), a biofilter (31,416 sq.ft), a secondary clarifier (15,394 sq.ft), a supernatant holding lagoon (15,000 sq.ft), two aeration basins (7,360 sq.ft), two final clarifiers (10,053 sq.ft), two EQ tanks (8,970 sq.ft), and four filter cells (960 sq.ft) which are all exposed to rainfall intrusion and/or rainwater runoff. The total process square footage does not account for the areas at the WRRF that are within containment. Containment areas gravity flow to multiple sumps throughout the plant which pump back to the beginning of the treatment process after the Parshall flumes where influent is totalized. To add, treated process water (3W) is used for washdowns. 3W makes up a portion of the effluent; however, this water is not metered and cannot be extrapolated from our effluent flow.

The Sunnyvale Water Pollution Control Plant (Global ID NPD100051562) has 440 acres of Oxidation Ponds that form the backbone of its secondary treatment process. In doing so, they also create tremendous storage capacity, such that what comes into the plant does not necessarily go out in the same day, week, or even month. They actually average a 30-45 day detention time. Due to their large surface area, evaporation rates are also high especially in the warmer months, further confounding influent and effluent flow rates.Toward the end of July 2020, the WPCP experienced a rupture of its secondary effluent pipeline, resulting in the emergency need to temporarily cease NPDES discharge and store influent flows in the Oxidation Ponds in order to establish bypass pumping. Discharge resumed in August 2020 under an alternate flow configuration reliant on repurposing existing process piping, which bypassed the ruptured secondary effluent line and allowed Sunnyvale to construct an intermediate solution. Consequently, recycled water production was ceased for the remainder of 2020. This incident further increased the difference between influent and effluent flows for the remainder of 2020.

In doing so, they also create tremendous storage capacity, such that what comes into the plant does not necessarily go out in the same day, week, or even month. They actually average a 30-45 day detention time. Due to their large surface area, evaporation rates are also high especially in the warmer months, further confounding influent and effluent flow rates.Toward the end of July 2020, the WPCP experienced a rupture of its secondary effluent pipeline, resulting in the emergency need to temporarily cease NPDES discharge and store influent flows in the Oxidation Ponds in order to establish bypass pumping. Discharge resumed in August 2020 under an alternate flow configuration reliant on repurposing existing process piping, which bypassed the ruptured secondary effluent line and allowed Sunnyvale to construct an intermediate solution. Consequently, recycled water production was ceased for the remainder of 2020. This incident further increased the difference between influent and effluent flows for the remainder of 2020.

The Sunnyvale Water Pollution Control Plant (Global ID NPD100051562) has 400 acres of Oxidation Ponds that form the backbone of its secondary treatment process. In doing so, they also create tremendous storage capacity, such that what comes into the plant does not necessarily go out in the same day, week, or even month. They actually average a 30-45 day detention time. Due to their large surface area, evaporation rates are also high especially in the warmer months, further confounding influent and effluent flow rates. The WPCP temporarily suspended recycled water production periodically in 2021 due to challenges in meeting turbidity limits. The WPCP observed a species of single-cell algae belonging to the picoplankton class that rapidly began to dominate the community in the Oxidation Ponds and outcompete other algae species that are generally easier to remove in clarifiers. The emergence of this new species created significant operational challenges in meeting the 2 NTU requirement for turbidity. The current polymer being used at the WPCP, which has been applied successfully for nearly a decade, was less effective at promoting the formation of large flocs of the novel species. The City is in the process of reevaluating its current polymer and other process controls in response to the challenging circumstances.

The WPCP temporarily suspended recycled water production periodically in 2021 due to challenges in meeting turbidity limits. The WPCP observed a species of single-cell algae belonging to the picoplankton class that rapidly began to dominate the community in the Oxidation Ponds and outcompete other algae species that are generally easier to remove in clarifiers. The emergence of this new species created significant operational challenges in meeting the 2 NTU requirement for turbidity. The current polymer being used at the WPCP, which has been applied successfully for nearly a decade, was less effective at promoting the formation of large flocs of the novel species. The City is in the process of reevaluating its current polymer and other process controls in response to the challenging circumstances.

The Sunnyvale Water Pollution Control Plant (Global ID NPD100051562) has 400 acres of Oxidation Ponds that form the backbone of its secondary treatment process. In doing so, they also create tremendous storage capacity, such that what comes into the plant does not necessarily go out in the same day, week, or even month. They actually average a 30-45 day detention time. Due to their large surface area, evaporation rates are also high especially in the warmer months, further confounding influent and effluent flow rates. The WPCP temporarily suspended recycled water production periodically in 2021 due to challenges in meeting turbidity limits. The WPCP observed a species of single-cell algae belonging to the picoplankton class that rapidly began to dominate the community in the Oxidation Ponds and outcompete other algae species that are generally easier to remove in clarifiers. The emergence of this new species created significant operational challenges in meeting the 2 NTU requirement for turbidity. The current polymer being used at the WPCP, which has been applied successfully for nearly a decade, was less effective at promoting the formation of large flocs of the novel species. The City is in the process of reevaluating its current polymer and other process controls in response to the challenging circumstances.

The Sunnyvale Water Pollution Control Plant (Global ID NPD100051562) has 400 acres of Oxidation Ponds that form the backbone of its secondary treatment process. In doing so, they also create tremendous storage capacity, such that what comes into the plant does not necessarily go out in the same day, week, or even month. They actually average a 30-45 day detention time. Due to their large surface area, evaporation rates are also high especially in the warmer months, further confounding influent and effluent flow rates. The WPCP temporarily suspended recycled water production periodically in 2021 due to challenges in meeting turbidity limits. The WPCP observed a species of single-cell algae belonging to the picoplankton class that rapidly began to dominate the community in the Oxidation Ponds and outcompete other algae species that are generally easier to remove in clarifiers. The emergence of this new species created significant operational challenges in meeting the 2 NTU requirement for turbidity. The current polymer being used at the WPCP, which has been applied successfully for nearly a decade, was less effective at promoting the formation of large flocs of the novel species. The City is in the process of reevaluating its current polymer and other process controls in response to the challenging circumstances.

The Sunnyvale Water Pollution Control Plant (Global ID NPD100051562) has 400 acres of Oxidation Ponds that form the backbone of its secondary treatment process. In doing so, they also create tremendous storage capacity, such that what comes into the plant does not necessarily go out in the same day, week, or even month. They actually average a 30-45 day detention time. Due to their large surface area, evaporation rates are also high especially in the warmer months, further confounding influent and effluent flow rates. The WPCP temporarily suspended recycled water production periodically in 2021 due to challenges in meeting turbidity limits. The WPCP observed a species of single-cell algae belonging to the picoplankton class that rapidly began to dominate the community in the Oxidation Ponds and outcompete other algae species that are generally easier to remove in clarifiers. The emergence of this new species created significant operational challenges in meeting the 2 NTU requirement for turbidity. The current polymer being used at the WPCP, which has been applied successfully for nearly a decade, was less effective at promoting the formation of large flocs of the novel species. The City is in the process of reevaluating its current polymer and other process controls in response to the challenging circumstances.
